newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba prepared for possible U.S. attack - minister.
newsitem.headline: Cuba prepared for possible U.S. attack - minister.

text.p: Defence Minister Raul Castro said on Monday Cuba still faced a military threat from U.S. groups that wanted to provoke civil disorder on the island to justify a military invasion.

But Castro, who is also vice-president and the younger brother of President Fidel Castro, said that despite problems caused by the collapse of Cuba's old economic and military partner, the former Soviet Union, the Communist-ruled island was well prepared to meet any such threat.

He spoke in an interview with the weekly trade union newspaper Trabajadores to mark the 40th anniversay of Cuba's Revolutionary Armed Forces. The anniversary was being celebrated with a military parade in Havana's Revolution Square on Monday, presided over by the two Castro brothers.

Raul Castro said in the interview that Cuba "must never rule out the possibility of a direct military action (from the United States)." He said the most aggressive anti-Cuba sectors in the United States sought to provoke -- by squeezing Cuba economically -- civil disorder and a large-scale exodus of boat people similar to the Mariel boatlift of 1980, which would then be "a pretext for their military intervention."

But he said military leaders in the United States were aware that "firstly Cuba constitutes no threat to the national security of the United States, secondly that the price to pay in U.S. lives would be very high."
Washington maintains a 34-year-old economic embargo on Cuba, seeking to pressure Fidel Castro's government.

Asked about the perception that Cuba's military capability had been debilitated by economic difficulties and a lack of supplies, the defence minister said Cuba had increased its network of underground defence tunnels, was producing ammunition, mines and some weapons and had trained thousands of soldiers and militia members in recent years.

These efforts would not be wasted even if there were never a military confrontation with the United States, he said, adding that the state of preparedness was useful in dissuading any aggressive plans. "We don't want war but to build in peace a future well-being for our people," he said.

Cuba's armed forces day marks Dec. 2, 1956, when Fidel Castro, then 30, disembarked with some 82 rebels from the boat Granma in eastern Cuba to launch the guerrilla war that toppled former dictator Fulgencio Batista in January 1959.
